items.title: McCarthy was censured by his own Senate in 1954
items.claim: How did Joseph McCarthy's anti-communist campaign end?

options.text: After televised Army-McCarthy hearings exposed his methods, the Senate voted 67-22 to censure him on 2 December 1954; he died of liver failure in 1957 aged 48
He resigned and joined the Republican Party leadership

items.reveal:
McCarthy had risen on a 1950 Wheeling speech claiming 205 communists in the State Department. The Army-McCarthy hearings (April-June 1954) were televised; Army counsel Joseph Welch's 'Have you no sense of decency, sir?' on 9 June became the iconic moment.

Edward R. Murrow's CBS broadcast 'See It Now' on 9 March 1954 had already turned mainstream opinion. The Senate censure vote followed in December.

HUAC (House Un-American Activities Committee), the Hollywood blacklist, loyalty oaths and the Smith Act prosecutions continued separately and outlasted McCarthy.
items.why: McCarthyism as a phenomenon was bigger than McCarthy. His fall did not end the Red Scare — but it ended one specific style of grandstanding accusation, and television was central to both his rise and fall.

items.title: The Berlin Wall fell partly because of a press-conference error
items.claim: How did the Berlin Wall come to open on 9 November 1989?

options.text: Soviet troops dismantled it overnight on Gorbachev's orders

East German official Günter Schabowski announced new travel rules at a 6 p.m. press conference; asked when they took effect, he said 'as far as I know, immediately'; East Berliners massed at checkpoints and crossings opened without orders
Mass armed insurrection overwhelmed border guards
West German forces breached the wall by force

items.reveal:
The East German politburo had agreed new travel rules on 9 November 1989, intended to take effect the following day with bureaucratic processing. Schabowski had not been briefed in detail. Asked by Italian journalist Riccardo Ehrman 'when does this take effect?', he shuffled papers and said 'Sofort, unverzüglich' — immediately, without delay.

Within hours East Berliners gathered at the Bornholmer Strasse crossing. Commander Harald Jäger received no orders and, faced with thousands of citizens, opened the barrier around 11.30 p.m.

Within months the regime collapsed. German reunification followed on 3 October 1990. The Soviet Union itself dissolved on 26 December 1991.
items.why: Major historical turning points can hinge on a botched press conference. The Wall's opening was not authorised in the way it happened — it was triggered by a misstatement that the crowd then made real.

items.title: Lenin tried to remove Stalin from his deathbed
items.claim: In late 1922 and early 1923, Lenin dictated a 'Testament' commenting on his potential successors. What did it say about Stalin?

options.text: It praised Stalin as the most capable administrator and probable successor
It called Stalin 'too rude' and proposed removing him from his post as General Secretary
It did not mention Stalin at all
It endorsed Stalin only as a temporary compromise with Trotsky

items.reveal_title: Suppressed by the man it condemned
items.reveal:
In a postscript dictated on 4 January 1923, Lenin wrote: 'Stalin is too rude and this defect... becomes intolerable in a Secretary-General. That is why I suggest that the comrades think about a way of removing Stalin from that post.'

After Lenin's death in January 1924, the Testament was read at the Central Committee but suppressed. Stalin offered to resign at the 13th Congress; the offer was rejected and the document was buried. It was not published in the USSR until 1956 under Khrushchev.
items.why: Stalin's consolidation of power was not authorised by Lenin — it was achieved despite Lenin's explicit, dying objection. The myth of Stalin as Lenin's chosen heir was built later.
